title: CFCs, the ozone hole and the Montreal Protocol

sources.title: CFCs and their substitutes in stratospheric ozone depletion
4 facts you might not know about ozone and the Montreal Protocol
UCI loses the legendary F. Sherwood Rowland (2012-03-11)
Facts and figures on ozone protection

facts.text: CFCs are made of carbon, chlorine and fluorine; they are nontoxic, nonflammable and inert in the lower atmosphere, which made them safe for most uses.
CFCs were used as refrigerants, in aerosol sprays, as blowing agents for foams and packing materials, and as solvents.
In 1974 F. Sherwood Rowland and Mario Molina, chemists at the University of California, published the idea that CFCs harm ozone.
High in the stratosphere, ultraviolet light breaks CFCs apart and releases chlorine, which destroys ozone.
The ozone layer lies about 7 to 25 miles above Earth and shields life from harmful ultraviolet radiation, which can cause skin cancer.
The aerosol industry pushed back hard against the idea, and some fellow scientists at first thought it went too far.
The U.S. National Academy of Sciences confirmed the findings in 1976, and the United States banned CFC aerosol sprays in 1978.
In May 1985 British Antarctic Survey scientists reported that ozone over Antarctica was disappearing each spring.
NASA satellite data confirmed the finding and showed that the hole covered the whole Antarctic continent.
The Montreal Protocol was adopted in 1987 to phase out ozone-depleting substances such as CFCs.
No other UN treaty has been ratified by all countries, as the Montreal Protocol has.
About 99 percent of the ozone-depleting substances controlled by the Protocol have been phased out.
CFC-12 stays in the atmosphere for about 100 years.
If the Protocol is followed, ozone should return to 1980 values around 2040 for most of the world, around 2045 over the Arctic and around 2066 over Antarctica.
The Antarctic ozone hole has become smaller and shallower since 2000, though it varies a lot from year to year.
HFCs, which replaced CFCs, harm ozone far less but are powerful greenhouse gases; the 2016 Kigali Amendment phases them down.
Rowland, Molina and Paul Crutzen shared the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their work on ozone.
